subsection.name: Writing the model
subsection.p: A model object represents an object in the application's "business domain", for example, a Product object in a sales application. A model can be implemented simply as a regular Javabean (with the default implementation). Scope accesses the properties of such a bean using the BeansPropertyManager, which will in turn use the Javabean APIs to invoke the model's public getters and setters when it needs access to the properties (for example when updating a View with the current state of the model to which it is bound).

The properties of a model are identified and accessed via Selectors: either with a string name or an integer index. This provides Scope with a generic, decoupled means to access the properties of model objects, although application code will usually use a model's public accessors directly.

An "active" model can implement the ModelChangeEventSource interface in which case it will fire events whenever its internal state changes. This allows (for example) a Swing GUI to automatically update to show the latest state of the models that it presents.

subsection.name: Selectors
subsection.p: Selectors are identifiers for model properties. They are created by the factory methods Selector.fromString(java.lang.String) and Selector.fromInt(int). Properties can be identified by a String name (eg the "address" property of a Customer) or an integer index (eg element 1 of a List).

Selectors can be assembled in a list to identify a property in a model contained within another model. For example, the name of the pet of a Person. This Selector would be created by Selector.fromString("pet.name") and applied to a Person model object. Similarly, the name of a Person's first pet could be identified using Selector.fromString("pets.0.name") assuming that Person contains a List or array of Pets that contain a name property.

subsection.name: Model change events
subsection.p: Model change events notify their listeners that the model has changed. The listeners are typically components in an interactive View like a Swing GUI, or other models used as parent of the current model to have propagation of change events to the top-level model object.

subsection.name: Basic model
subsection.p:
Scope can use a simple JavaBean as its model, or even a basic datatype (String, Integer). You have the following choices at your disposal:
If your view displays a JavaBean, and if this bean is fully initialised and won't change while it is displayed in the view, you can use the JavaBean directly as the model. In the controller, write:
setModel(javabean);
If your want to update a bean being displayed and immediately see the change on the view, you need to subclass your bean from org.scopemvc.model.basic.BasicBean, and fire a model change event (using the fireModelChange method) when a property is modified.
In all cases, if there is a modification on a model and you want to see the latest changes in your view, you can always call explicitly the refresh() method on the view to refresh it with the latest model data.

section.name: Complex models
section.p: Scope supports the use of complex models, thanks to its Selector capabilities. A Scope Selector is used to identify a property in a model. They can also be compounded, so you can write Selector.fromString("pet.name") to access the name of the pet for a Person.

subsection.name: Lists, arrays and collection used as models
subsection.p:
Scope provides wrappers for most standard java.util Collection classes and also for object arrays.
See the org.scopemvc.model.collection package for more details.
